name: Function Calling Basics
question: How does a model actually use a tool?
summary: Each tool is a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its inputs. The model does not run anything: it returns a structured call, your code validates and runs it, and you send the result back under the same call id. The loop repeats until the model answers in text. tool_choice sets whether the model may, must or must not call a tool.
useCases: Any agent that must read live data or act: balances, orders, tickets
Turning free text into validated, typed arguments for an API
Replacing guesses with lookups, such as a UTR status check

items.detail: request with tools → tool_use → run it → tool_result → repeat until end_turn
auto (default with tools), any, tool (force one), none
each result carries the tool_use_id (OpenAI: call_id) of its call
strict: true constrains sampling so inputs always match the schema
a failed call goes back as a tool_result with is_error: true, never dropped
OpenAI suggests fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn

steps: Write each tool as a name, a 3–4 sentence description and an input schema
Send tools with tool_choice auto; force a tool only when the step truly requires it
Validate the arguments, run the tool, and return every result under its own call id
Cap the loop with a step limit and return errors with is_error so the model can recover
pitfalls: Forcing a tool on every turn wastes calls and can stop the model from answering
Mismatched or reused call ids break the conversation
Some current models reject tool_choice any and tool with a 400 error, as does manual extended thinking
remember: The model asks; your code runs. Match every result to its call id.
caption: Illustrative numbers. One lookup costs one extra model turn: 2 turns, 1 call.

code.text: "description": ("Look up a UPI payment by its 12-digit UTR number. "
"Use it whenever the user asks if a payment went through. "
"Never guess a status; ask for the UTR if it is missing. "
"Returns status, amount in INR and last update time."),
"strict": True,                          # inputs always match the schema
for turn in range(6):                        # step cap
break                                # the model answered in text
for block in (b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"):
out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)   # validate, then run

steps.title: Define the tool
steps.text: A name, a description of three or four sentences that says when to use it and when not, and a JSON Schema for the one argument, the UTR.

steps.title: Send tools and tool_choice
steps.text: The request carries the tool list and tool_choice auto, so the model may answer directly or call a tool. Forcing a call is only for steps that must produce one.

steps.title: Detect a tool call
steps.text: The response stops with stop_reason tool_use and contains a tool_use block: an id (toolu_01), the tool name and the arguments. The model has run nothing.

steps.title: Validate and run
steps.text: Your code checks the arguments against the schema and runs the lookup. With strict mode the arguments always match the schema, so this check rarely fails.

steps.title: Return the result under the same id
steps.text: Each tool_result carries the tool_use_id of the call it answers. A failure goes back too, with is_error true, so the model can recover instead of guessing.

steps.title: Loop with a step cap
steps.text: The loop sends the history back until the model answers in text. Here that is turn 2: one call, two model turns. The cap of 6 stops a runaway loop.

pros: Replaces guesses with lookups against live systems
Arguments arrive as validated, typed JSON rather than free text
The same loop works for one tool or fifty
Errors return to the model, which can often recover on its own
cons: Each sequential call adds a model turn and resends the history
A forced tool_choice can waste calls or block the answer
Loose schemas let malformed arguments through
Your code owns execution, timeouts and permissions
avoidWhen: The answer needs no live data or action
A fixed pipeline always calls the same API: call it directly, without the model

playgroundGuide.scenario: A UPI app’s support assistant has two tools: get_transaction_status (by UTR) and get_refund_status (by the refund id the first one returns). Users send three kinds of message: a thank-you that needs no tool, a status question that needs one lookup, and a refund question that needs two lookups in turn. The loop has a cap of 6 model turns.
controls: Pick the user message and the tool_choice setting: auto, any, tool (force get_transaction_status) or none.
Choose whether forcing applies to the first request only or to every request in the loop.
Choose a careful or sloppy model, and turn strict schemas on or off.

outputs.name: Model turns
outputs.meaning: Requests sent to the model, including the one that produces the final answer.

outputs.name: Tool calls made
outputs.meaning: Calls the model emitted, with how many the question needed and how many were wasted.

outputs.name: Schema-valid arguments
outputs.meaning: Calls whose arguments matched the input schema on the first try.

outputs.name: End state
outputs.meaning: Answered, answered without data (a guess), or stuck at the step cap.

outputs.name: Turn trace
outputs.meaning: What happened on each turn: a call (✓ valid, ✗ malformed), a repeated forced call, or the answer.

presets.name: Forced on a greeting

presets.name: Sloppy model, no strict

presets.name: Forced on every turn
presets.expect: tool_choice tool on every request: the lookup succeeds on turn 1, then 5 more forced calls follow and the loop stops at the cap of 6 turns without an answer.

presets.name: tool_choice none
presets.expect: The status question with no tools allowed: 1 turn and 0 calls, but the answer is a guess, not a lookup.

practice.scenario: A UPI app’s support assistant gets “Did my ₹1,200 payment go through?” with a pasted UTR number. Instead of guessing, the model calls get_transaction_status with the 12-digit UTR, the app runs the lookup against the payments switch, and the model answers from the returned status: two model turns, one call.

industries.use: Status checks on UPI, NEFT and card transactions by reference number
Look up a PNR before answering “Is my flight on time?”
Fetch the current plan and data balance before recommending a recharge

practice.analogy: A waiter taking an order. The waiter writes the dish on a ticket in the kitchen’s format; the kitchen cooks it; the waiter brings back exactly that plate to the table that ordered it.

library.name: Anthropic SDK (tool use)
library.what: Pass tools with JSON Schemas; the response contains tool_use blocks that you run and answer with tool_result blocks.

practice.note: Minimal loop. get_transaction_status stands for your own lookup. Check the docs for current model names and strict-schema support.

samples.code:
import json, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

tools = [{
    "name": "get_transaction_status",
    "description": ("Look up the status of a UPI payment by its 12-digit UTR number. "
                    "Use it whenever the user asks whether a payment succeeded, failed or was reversed. "
                    "Never guess a status; if the user has not given a UTR, ask for it. "
                    "Returns status, amount in INR and the time of the last update."),
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"utr": {"type": "string", "description": "12-digit UTR"}},
                     "required": ["utr"], "additionalProperties": False},
    "strict": True,                                   # inputs always match the schema
}]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Did UTR 412345678901 go through?"}]
for step in range(6):                                 # step cap
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, tool_choice={"type": "auto"}, messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        print(next(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")); break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for b in resp.content:
        if b.type != "tool_use":
            continue
        try:
            out = get_transaction_status(**b.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": json.dumps(out)})
        except Exception as e:                        # send the failure back, don't drop it
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                            "content": f"Lookup failed: {e}", "is_error": True})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

numericDrill.question: A question needs 3 lookups, each depending on the one before, with tool_choice auto. Every turn resends 2,000 tokens of prompt and tool definitions, and each tool result adds 300 tokens that stay in the history. Ignoring the model’s own output, how many input tokens does the whole exchange use?
numericDrill.answer: 3 calls in sequence plus the final answer = 4 turns. Turn 1: 2,000. Turn 2: 2,300. Turn 3: 2,600. Turn 4: 2,900. Total 9,800 input tokens. Each extra sequential call adds a turn that resends everything.

interview.question: Walk me through what happens when a model “calls a tool”.
interview.answer: The model never executes anything. You send tool definitions (name, description, input schema). If the model decides to use one, the response stops with stop_reason tool_use and contains a structured call with an id and arguments. Your code validates and runs it, then sends a tool_result carrying the same id. The model continues, possibly calling more tools, until it answers in text.

interview.question: When would you use tool_choice any or tool, and what are the risks?
interview.answer: Force a tool only when the step must produce a structured call, such as an extraction step, and usually only for the first turn. Forcing on a greeting wastes a call, and leaving it forced in a loop can stop the model from ever answering. Some current models and manual extended thinking reject any and tool, so check the docs and fall back to auto.

mistakes.mistake: Setting every tool_use_id to the first block’s id
mistakes.fix: Return each result under the id of the call it answers

mistakes.mistake: Dropping a failed call from the results
mistakes.fix: Return it as a tool_result with is_error: true and a clear message

quiz.question: A UPI app’s assistant is asked “Did UTR 412345678901 go through?” It has a get_transaction_status tool. What does the model actually return when it decides to use the tool?
options: The payment status, fetched from the switch
A tool_use block with an id, the tool name and the UTR as an argument
A Python function call that the API runs on your server
A request for your database credentials
quiz.explanation: The model never runs tools. It returns a structured call; your code executes it and returns the result.

quiz.question: Your code runs a balance lookup and sends back the result. What must the tool_result block contain so the model can use it?
options: The tool name only
The tool_use_id of the call it answers
The full original request
A new system prompt
quiz.explanation: Each result is matched to its call by id; without the right tool_use_id the result cannot be attributed.

quiz.question: A recharge assistant greets a user who says “Thanks, bye!”. The request uses tool_choice any on every turn. What happens?
options: The model says goodbye
The model is forced to call a tool on every turn and cannot reply in text
The API ignores tool_choice for greetings
The model calls every tool once and then answers
quiz.explanation: any requires a tool call in each response, so a loop that always sends it never lets the model answer in text.

quiz.question: A PNR-status question needs one lookup. With tool_choice auto, how many model turns does the exchange take, including the answer?
quiz.explanation: Turn 1 returns the call; after your code sends the result, turn 2 is the answer.

quiz.question: A claims assistant’s model sometimes sends policy_no as a number instead of the string the schema requires. What is the most direct fix?
options: Lower the temperature
Turn on strict schemas so sampling is constrained to the schema
Add “please use strings” to the system prompt
Increase max_tokens
quiz.explanation: Strict mode uses grammar-constrained sampling so inputs always match the schema.

quiz.question: An order-tracking tool throws a timeout. What should your loop send back?
options: Nothing; skip that call
A tool_result for that call with is_error true and a short message
A fabricated “delivered” status
A new user message asking the model to try again
quiz.explanation: Every call needs a result; an error result lets the model retry, try another path or explain.

quiz.question: A brokerage assistant defines get_holdings. Which belong in a good tool definition? Select all that apply.
options: A name that says what it does
A description of when to use it and when not
A JSON Schema for the inputs
The user’s password for the trading API
quiz.explanation: Name, description and input schema define a tool. Credentials stay in your executor, never in the definition.

quiz.question: A lab-report assistant has a step whose only job is to extract fields into a record_vitals call. When is forcing that tool reasonable?
options: On every turn of every conversation
For that one extraction step, typically on the first request only
Never; forcing is not supported
Only when the model is uncertain
quiz.explanation: Forcing a specific tool suits a step that must produce a structured call; afterwards switch back to auto.

quiz.question: A question needs 3 dependent lookups. Each turn resends 2,000 tokens of prompt and tool definitions, and each tool result adds 300 tokens that stay in the history. Ignoring model output, how many input tokens does the exchange use?
An OpenAI-based assistant returns function results. Which field ties a function output to the call it answers?
options: function_name
call_id
response_id
thread_id
quiz.explanation: OpenAI matches outputs to calls by call_id, as Anthropic does with tool_use_id.

quiz.question: A loan assistant’s loop sometimes never ends. Which safeguards help? Select all that apply.
options: A step cap on model turns
Stopping forcing a tool after the first request
Returning errors as is_error so the model can conclude
Removing all tool descriptions
quiz.explanation: A cap bounds the loop, forcing only once lets the model answer, and error results let it wrap up. Removing descriptions makes things worse.

quiz.question: With tool_choice none, a student asks “What is my exam hall number?” and a lookup tool exists. What happens?
options: The model calls the tool anyway
The model answers without calling any tool, so it cannot know the hall
The API returns an error
The tool is called automatically by the API
quiz.explanation: none prevents tool calls, so a question that needs data gets an answer without it.

quiz.question: An engineer sets tool_choice {"type":"tool","name":"refund"} and gets HTTP 400 on one current model with extended thinking enabled. What is the likely cause?
options: The refund tool has too long a description
Forcing a specific tool is not supported in that configuration, so fall back to auto
The API key lacks refund permission
The model is overloaded
quiz.explanation: Forced tool_choice (any or tool) is not supported with extended thinking and is rejected by some current models.

quiz.question: Which statements about the tool loop are true? Select all that apply.
options: The model decides whether to call a tool when tool_choice is auto
Your application executes the tool
A response can contain more than one tool_use block
The model can read your database directly once a tool is defined
quiz.explanation: The model chooses, your code executes, and several calls can appear in one response. The model never gets direct access.

quiz.question: A policy tool’s schema uses a JSON Schema feature that strict mode does not support. What should you expect?
options: Strict mode silently ignores the feature and still guarantees validity
The request can be rejected; strict supports a subset of JSON Schema, so simplify the schema
The model ignores the whole schema
The tool is called without arguments
quiz.explanation: Strict mode supports only a subset of JSON Schema, so unsupported features must be removed or rewritten.

quiz.question: An agent runs 5,000 conversations a day. 40% need one lookup, 30% two sequential lookups and 30% none. With tool_choice auto, how many tool calls a day?
OpenAI’s guidance on how many functions to make available at the start of a turn is roughly what?
options: Fewer than 5
Fewer than 20
Up to 200
There is no guidance
quiz.explanation: OpenAI suggests keeping fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn for accuracy.

quiz.question: A clinic assistant’s calls sometimes fail validation. Which fixes address the arguments themselves? Select all that apply.
options: Enable strict schemas
Use enums and clear parameter descriptions
Raise max_tokens
Switch the loop to streaming output
quiz.explanation: Strict mode and clearer, constrained parameters improve argument validity; token limits and streaming do not.

quiz.question: Which benchmark is designed to score how accurately models form function calls, including parallel and multi-turn calls?
options: MMLU
BFCL
HumanEval
GSM8K
quiz.explanation: BFCL, the Berkeley function-calling benchmark, evaluates simple, multiple, parallel and multi-turn function calling.

quiz.question: Which situations are better served by calling an API directly from your code, without letting a model choose tools? Select all that apply.
options: A nightly job that always fetches the same shipment report
A fixed webhook that always posts a delivery status to one endpoint
A chat assistant answering open questions about orders
An agent that must decide which of several lookups a question needs
quiz.explanation: Fixed pipelines need no model decision. Open questions and choosing between lookups are where tool calling helps.
